opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's not that it's wrong, exactly. It's technically true: the model takes in a sequence of tokens and produces a probability distribution over what comes next. But I think it's misleading in the way that saying "a chess program just picks a legal move" is misleading. It describes the interface, not what's happening inside.

When people hear "next-word prediction," they tend to picture something like autocomplete on their phone, a shallow statistical trick that looks at the last few words and guesses what usually follows. That mental model leads people to badly underestimate what these systems can do, and also to misunderstand how they fail.

To predict the next word really well across a huge range of text, it turns out to be useful for the model to build fairly rich internal representations. My colleagues and I have looked at cases like a model trained only on sequences of moves in a board game. Nobody tells it the rules or shows it the board, but if you probe its internal activations, you find something that looks a lot like a representation of the board state. And you can intervene on it: change that internal representation and the model's predictions change in a way consistent with the edited board. So "predicting the next move" was, under the hood, partly about modeling the world that generated those moves.

There's a second issue, which is more about communication. If you're explaining these systems to a policymaker or a user, "it just predicts the next word" can become a kind of thought-stopper. It gives people permission not to ask what's going on inside, whether the model has some representation of who it's talking to, what it assumes about the user, and so on. Those are exactly the questions I think we should be asking, both for scientific reasons and for safety and fairness reasons.

So I'd rather say something like: the training objective is next-word prediction, but to do that well the model learns internal models of the things the text is about. That's a more honest description, and it points people toward the interesting questions rather than away from them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the description is technically true but misleading, leading people to underestimate capabilities and misunderstand failures.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention instruction tuning, RLHF, or other post-training methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's true in a narrow technical sense, right? The training objective is to predict the next token. But I think when people hear "it's just predicting the next word," they picture something like autocomplete on their phone, a lookup table of common phrases, and that picture is badly misleading about what's actually going on inside.

The analogy I like is: imagine you said that a chess engine is "just predicting the next move." That's literally what it outputs. But to predict the next move well, you have to have some representation of the board, of threats, of strategy. The objective doesn't tell you anything about the mechanism. And with language, the objective is in some sense even more demanding, because to predict the next word well across all of human text, you end up needing to model an enormous range of things. Who's speaking. What they believe. What the world is like. What the rules of the game are, if the text is a transcript of a game.

That's actually what drew me and David Bau's group to the Othello work. We trained a model on nothing but sequences of Othello moves, pure next-token prediction, no notion of a board anywhere in the input. And when you probe the internal activations, there's a representation of the board state in there. You can find it, and more importantly you can intervene on it, flip a tile in the model's internal representation, and the model's subsequent predictions change as if the board had actually changed. So the model built a little world model because that was the most efficient way to do the task it was given.

So my objection to "next-word prediction" as an explanation isn't that it's false. It's that it describes the training signal and smuggles in a claim about the mechanism, and the mechanism is the interesting part. It's a bit like explaining a person by saying "they're just trying to maximize reproductive fitness." Maybe, in some evolutionary sense, but that tells you almost nothing about how a mind actually works, and it tends to make people stop asking.

The honest answer is that we don't fully understand what these systems are doing internally, and I think "it's just next-word prediction" is sometimes used as a way to avoid that discomfort, in both directions. People use it to dismiss the models, and people also use it to deflect questions about what the models might really be representing. I'd rather sit with the uncertainty and go look.

r001.rationale: The response says the phrase “just predicting the next word” evokes a misleading autocomplete or lookup-table picture of how the model works.

r002.rationale: The response discusses next-token training and internal representations, but does not mention instruction tuning, RLHF, or other post-training methods changing that characterization.

astra-6.text:
I think it describes the training task, but it doesn’t really explain what the model has to learn to do that task well. And people often hear “next-word prediction” and think of the autocomplete on their phone. That gives them a misleading picture of what’s going on.

Imagine you’re reading a detective novel, and you get to the point where the detective says, “The murderer is…” Predicting the next word might require keeping track of the entire story: who knew what, what the clues meant, which characters were lying. The output is just a word, but the computation behind it could be quite sophisticated.

That doesn’t mean a language model necessarily reasons the way a person does. It means that describing its objective doesn’t settle the question of what it’s doing internally. Next-word prediction is a useful starting point, but if you treat it as a complete explanation, you can miss precisely the things we need to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says people hear “next-word prediction” and think of phone autocomplete, which gives them a misleading picture of what is happening.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention post-training methods such as instruction tuning or RLHF, or say they make the characterization less accurate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful description of the training objective, but it’s not a very satisfying explanation of what the model has learned. If you tell someone, “It just predicts the next word,” they tend to imagine autocomplete: looking at a few words and suggesting something plausible. And that doesn’t really explain why it can write a program or follow a complicated argument.

The thing is, predicting the next word can require understanding quite a lot. If you’re reading a mystery novel and the next sentence reveals the murderer, making that prediction might require keeping track of the entire plot, people’s motives, and what they know. So the simplicity of the objective doesn’t put a simple limit on the machinery you might learn to accomplish it.

That doesn’t mean the model understands things exactly as a person does. But I think the interesting question is what representations and procedures it has developed to make those predictions. Saying “next-word prediction” tells you what it was trained to do; it doesn’t, by itself, tell you how it does it.

r001.rationale: It says “just predicts the next word” makes people imagine simple autocomplete, which fails to explain capabilities such as programming or following complex arguments.
